disclosures.name: TestValuePointerAndUnsafePointer/channel
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: reflect's pointer projection and a raw memory-word read are separate authorities in the managed model, and this assert compares them. Go has one mechanism for both because its pointers ARE addresses; go2cs cannot, and each side's rule exists because the alternative was measured and hurt. The want comes from golib's `implicit operator uintptr(ж<T>)` (EnsureStableAddress, then `fixed (&value.Value)`), which must hand back a REAL PINNED, DEREFERENCEABLE address -- Go permits converting the scalar back and dereferencing it, which go/types' check_test.go does, and the uintptr arm's exact fidelity rests on it. The got comes from reflect's own reflectPointerToken, which must hand back an OPAQUE STABLE PER-OBJECT IDENTITY: a map or slice value is a header struct freshly boxed on every read, so an address-based token differs per read and encoding/json's cycle detector stops matching entries it stored itself (the recorded 0xc00000fd stack-exhaustion defect), while typeDescriptorOrderToken's packed type names are what make fmt.Println(map[I]int{...}) print deterministically. Measured 2026-08-31: the six wants cluster at ~2.993e12 within a few hundred bytes (consecutively allocated boxes, real addresses) while the gots scatter over 2.7e7-2.1e9 (32-bit identity hashes) -- the two sides already share the ManagedPointerTokens registry, so what differs is the MINT, not resolution. Unifying either direction sacrifices a banked behavior worth hundreds of verdicts for six rows. The operation under test is correct; the architecture is showing through.

disclosures.name: TestChanAlloc
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: want-zero AllocsPerRun assert on channel send/recv through reflect. The managed channel carries its element boxed, so a send allocates where Go copies into the ring buffer.

disclosures.name: TestDeepEqualAllocs/[6]uint8
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: want-zero AllocsPerRun assert over DeepEqual of two identical values. Go proves both operands non-escaping and runs the comparison with no mallocs; the managed bridge boxes each operand into the interface DeepEqual takes, which is a CLR heap allocation per run and the one structural object the assert forbids. The CLR publishes no in-process malloc counter, so the reported figure is golib-site count, a LOWER bound.

Go proves both operands non-escaping and runs the comparison with no mallocs; the managed bridge boxes each operand into the interface DeepEqual takes, which is a CLR heap allocation per run and the one structural object the assert forbids. The CLR publishes no in-process malloc counter, so the reported figure is golib-site count, a LOWER bound.

disclosures.name: TestMapAlloc
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: bounded AllocsPerRun assert on map assignment through reflect. The managed map stores boxed keys and values, so each assignment allocates where Go writes into the bucket in place.

disclosures.name: TestMapIterReset
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: want-zero AllocsPerRun assert on MapIter.Reset. Go reuses one hiter in place; the managed iterator must obtain a fresh enumerator from the map when it rebinds, because IEnumerator carries no reset-to-a-different-source operation. The allocation is the enumerator itself, charged outside golib (BCL internal), so the figure is reported in BYTES rather than as a count.

disclosures.name: TestMapIterSet
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: want-zero AllocsPerRun assert on SetIterKey/SetIterValue. Go writes the entry through hiter with no allocation; the managed path reads the enumerator Current, which the BCL materializes as a KeyValuePair box per step. Reaching this assert at all is the correct behavior -- the same test previously failed before the operation ran.

disclosures.name: TestSmallZero
disclosures.reason: alloc-profile: want-zero AllocsPerRun assert on reflect.Zero for small values. Go returns a value whose data word fits inline and allocates nothing; the managed bridge must materialize a boxed zero for the same Value.

disclosures.name: TestSliceAt
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: reflect.SliceAt builds a slice that aliases the pointer's memory faithfully (len/cap/nil and the negative/nil-pointer/overflow panics all agree with Go), but its Value.Pointer() is a STORAGE-IDENTITY token -- HashCode.Combine(backing, low), kept stable for encoding/json's cycle detector and internal/fmtsort's map ordering -- while uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p[0])) is the pinned data address. The two are managed-model projections of one storage that coincide only for native memory; making them equal would pin managed storage on every Pointer() call and move the cycle-detector hot path off its cheap hash, so the identity is disclosed rather than unified (coordinator ruling 2026-09-02; token-unification refused).

disclosures.name: TestGCBits
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the verifyGCBitsSlice path compares a slice's HEAP-ALLOCATION GC bitmap. Go's gcbits(*E) reads the heap object at the pointer and returns the element's pointer bits REPEATED by the allocation's size class -- have [1] want [1 1], have [1] want [1 1 ...x10000], have [0 1] want [0 1 0 1]. The managed gcbits answers from the POINTEE TYPE's layout (GoReflect.GoGCMaskOf) -- the element's bits ONCE -- because the managed model has no allocation size class to repeat by, and reflect.NewAt's *E carries no cap it was never given. The non-slice verifyGCBits path (New(typ).Interface()) is unaffected. Same managed-model class as the alloc-count and pointer-identity disclosures (coordinator ruling 2026-09-02; C2's gcbits authority, R mints the reflect manifest entry).

disclosures.name: TestPtrToGC
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the row converts **uintptr to a DEFINED pointer type. A defined pointer type emits as a go2cs-gen wrapper CLASS rather than as the box the outer slot holds, so no aliasing view of that slot exists to hand out and the conversion cannot be performed at all -- increment E3 refused it BY NAME rather than approximating it, which is why the panic names both types. Go performs it because its pointer is an address and the conversion reinterprets one word; a managed host has no word to reinterpret. Measured at E3 root 5 and again at the 7g tree.

disclosures.name: TestAlignment
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the assert compares reflect's StructField.Offset against an offset the TEST computes itself, by subtracting uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&x)) from uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&x.field)). Managed memory exposes no stable byte offsets to that arithmetic -- go2cs pointers are stable identity TOKENS, the same model the guintptr hand-conversion rests on -- so the test's own subtraction yields 0 where Go yields the field's offset. reflect's Offset is CORRECT here and is not what this row measures: the reading is 'mismatched offsets in structure alignment: 8 0', the 8 being the bridge's right answer and the 0 the arithmetic the host cannot support.

disclosures.name: TestCallReturnsEmpty
disclosures.reason: codegen-liveness: the row's own line is `v := ValueOf(f).Call(nil)[0]`, whose intermediate []Value is NEVER NAMED. Go drops that temporary at its last use, so the second result -- the *[2]int64 whose finalizer the test waits on -- becomes unreachable and the finalizer runs. Our host keeps the caller's frame slot rooted while the intermediate remains in scope, so the second result survives the collection and the 5-second wait reports Go's own message. Same mechanism as unique's TestMakeClonesStrings, measured by the same one-axis discriminator. ARMS, Go first then Release+TC0: (a) the row's line VERBATIM -- COLLECTED / RETAINED; (b) the same line with the intermediate NAMED and CLEARED before the collection -- COLLECTED / COLLECTED. One axis, the frame slot. ALIASING EXONERATION, stated explicitly because it is what makes this entry safe: this test exists to catch Go issue 21717, a zero-sized return aliasing the NEXT return's storage. If our implementation had that alias, clearing the slice could NOT have helped -- the taken value still holds out[0] and is KeepAlive'd across the collection -- so arm (b) would have read RETAINED. It read COLLECTED. The defect this test was written to detect is therefore measurably ABSENT in our Call, and this entry cannot hide it. LIMIT, stated so the boundary is inherited rather than inferred: the arm pair was measured at Release+TC0 ONLY. Retention under tiering and in Debug is PREDICTED by the sibling row's measured tier behaviour (an overwritten slot is honoured at Release+TC0 and not under tiering or Debug) and was NOT run for this row.
